This page is the way into the format. It gives the principles, shows what a
data file holds, and says what review is asked for and what has been tested.
Most of it is folded: open what you want to read.

The format is a set of names and rules on top of a standard MuData file.
Nothing in it is specific to one analysis tool. One tool that builds on it is
sceptre, whose analyses of a data file are stored in the
[sceptre analysis format](https://raw.githack.com/Katsevich-Lab/sceptre-hub/main/sceptre-analysis-format/notebook.html).

Two reference documents sit behind this page: [`SPEC.md`](https://github.com/Katsevich-Lab/sceptre-hub/blob/main/perturb-seq-data-format/SPEC.md)
has the rules, numbered, and [`RATIONALE.md`](https://github.com/Katsevich-Lab/sceptre-hub/blob/main/perturb-seq-data-format/RATIONALE.md)
has the full reasons, with evidence, under the same numbers.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Draft.** Nothing here has been reviewed. The format is version 0.1 until it
is frozen as 1.0.
:::

## The principles

Every choice in the format follows from these eight. Where two of them pull
apart, the earlier one wins. Open one for its reason and what follows from it.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(nt.principles("RATIONALE.md", "https://github.com/Katsevich-Lab/sceptre-hub/blob/main/perturb-seq-data-format/RATIONALE.md", "## 2. The eight principles"))
```

## What is on disk

A screen is **one file**: a standard MuData `.h5mu` file, written once and
never modified. It holds raw counts and what is known about the cells and the
gRNAs, and nothing an analysis computes. The tree below is read from the
example in `example/highmoi/`. Open a group to see what is in it, and an entry
to see what it holds.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(nt.screen_tree())
```

## Open the file yourself

Standard libraries read it, in R or Python.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
screen <- MuData::readH5MU("example/highmoi/screen.h5mu")
screen
```

## Python

```{python}
import mudata

screen = mudata.read_h5mu("example/highmoi/screen.h5mu")
print(screen)
```

:::

## The choices to review

These are the choices that cannot change after the format is frozen without
breaking existing files. Disagreement is cheap now and costly then. Each opens
to its reason and the alternative it was chosen over; the label after each
is the section of `RATIONALE.md` (and of `SPEC.md`) with the detail.

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Data and analysis are separate.</strong> <span class="where">S12</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The data file holds nothing an analysis produces: no assignments, no kept-or-removed flag, no results. Each analysis is its own folder.
- **Why.** One dataset has many analyses, and the data file is then written once and never touched again. Keeping a kept-or-removed flag in the data file, as public pysceptre does, means rewriting the whole file to work on the kept cells.
- **Instead of.** One self-contained file holding data, assignments and results, which is the IGVF pipeline's layout and suits uploading one file to a portal.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>The data is one MuData <code>.h5mu</code> file.</strong> <span class="where">S1</span></summary>

- **Why.** MuData is the scverse standard for one set of cells measured in several ways. Standard libraries open it in both languages, and one file is easy to move and publish.
- **Instead of.** A Zarr store, two `.h5ad` files, the `ondisc` format, or a folder of Parquet and matrix files.
- **Locks in.** HDF5. A Zarr variant could be added later without changing anything else.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Counts are stored by feature.</strong> <span class="where">S3</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The count matrix is cells × features, column-compressed, so one gene is one contiguous read.
- **Why.** Every stage works gene by gene. With counts stored by cell, the IGVF pipeline first splits the whole file into per-gene chunk files.
- **Cost.** A file from another tool is usually stored by cell and is converted once at import.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Modalities are named for what was measured, and the analysis says which one it tests.</strong> <span class="where">S2, A1</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The gRNA modality is always `grna`. Every other modality is named for its measurement (`rna`, `protein`, ...). `analysis.json` names the response modality; nothing finds it by a fixed name.
- **Why.** A file can then hold a second measured modality, and any modality can become the response of a later analysis.
- **Instead of.** A fixed role name such as `response`, which is what both packages use in memory today.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Covariate names carry the modality's name: <code>rna_n_umis</code>, not <code>response_n_umis</code>.</strong> <span class="where">S5</span></summary>

- **The choice.** Facts about the cell (batch, donor) are in the shared cell table. Measurements of a modality are in that modality's cell table. A model's covariate table prefixes each modality's columns with its name.
- **Why.** A batch belongs to the cell, not to its RNA. A role prefix cannot name the RNA depth in an analysis whose response is protein.
- **Cost.** Formulas users write today say `response_n_umis`. The packages can keep accepting that name and translate.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>The file's own entries are at the top level of <code>uns</code>.</strong> <span class="where">S10</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The format version (`perturb_seq_format`), the dataset's identifier (`dataset_id`) and what is known about the screen (`title`, `organism`, `genome_build`, `perturbation_type`, `source`) are scalar entries at the top level of `uns`.
- **Why.** They are facts about the dataset, so other tools should be able to read and write them. Under a key named for one tool they would belong to that tool.
- **The version** is `MAJOR.MINOR`. A minor increase adds something older software can ignore. A major increase is any change after which older software could misread a file, and software refuses a major version it does not know.
- **Not in the file.** Whether a screen is treated as low or high multiplicity of infection. It selects an analysis's defaults, so it belongs to the analysis.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>The names.</strong> <span class="where">SPEC, section 2</span></summary>

Names are as hard to change as structure: the modality names `rna` and `grna`, and the columns `grna_target`, `target_chr`, `target_start`, `target_end`, `vector_id`, `n_umis`, `n_nonzero`, `p_mito`. Other formats use other names for the same things, and none is a standard. If one reads wrongly to you, now is the time to say so.

</details>

## Questions for reviewers

1. **Is anything missing that a real screen needs?** For gRNA annotation the format has a target, its position and an optional vector, and no gRNA type or spacer sequence yet. It defines no annotation of genes.
2. **Coordinates.** Target positions are 1-based with both ends included, as in GTF files, and a file with positions has to say which genome build they are in. Is that the right convention?
3. **Limits.** A gRNA has one target, and so does a vector carrying several gRNAs; combinatorial screens are refused. DNA-targeting is assumed. Are those limits acceptable for now?
4. **The matrix layout.** Counts are stored by feature, which suits fitting one gene at a time. Files from mapping pipelines and from scanpy are stored by cell. Should the format allow both and recommend one?
5. **The required columns.** Every modality's cell table must have `n_umis` and `n_nonzero`. Is that the right minimum for software other than sceptre?
6. **The names.** Would you use `rna` and `grna`, `grna_target`, and the entry names at the top level of `uns`, or do the names of another format serve better?

<details class="fold">
<summary>What does not need review now</summary>

These can be added or changed later without breaking any file.

- **Optional columns not yet in the format:** gRNA type, spacer, gene annotation (`RATIONALE.md`, planned additions).
- **The wording of individual rules.** The sorting into file rules, behaviour rules and guidance is meant to be final; the sentences are not.
- **Compression settings.** Software reading the files does not depend on them.
- **The code in `format/`.** The validators show that the rules can be checked in both languages; the writer is temporary.
- **The comparisons with IGVF and pertpy** in `RATIONALE.md`, unless you know those formats and see an error.

</details>

## What has been tested

`verify/run.sh` runs every check. It uses no analysis tool. The counts below
are from the run this page was rendered after.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(nt.status({
    "conformance": "Both validators report exactly the expected rules on every data file of `conformance/` (files that conform, and files that each break a rule), and the standard readers read the files that must still be read",
    "encodings": "Every kind of value, written by each language's standard libraries and read by the other's. The kinds the format allows come back correct; the kinds it forbids still break",
    "independent-readers": "Tools outside this code read the files: anndata and scanpy in Python, HDF5Array in R",
    "wide-index": "The 64-bit branch of the count matrix's index type, with the limit lowered because no test file reaches it",
}))
```

- **Once, at scale:** on a real screen of 207,324 cells, written by both languages to identical files and read back in memory and from disk (`scale-test/`).
- **On three operating systems:** the suite passes on macOS, Linux and Windows.

**Not tested.**

- Real data in a second measured modality.
- Count matrices past the 32-bit index limit. The 64-bit types are handled; values that large are not exercised.
- An implementation by someone else. One author wrote the specification and both validators.

`SPEC.md` marks each rule with how it is checked, including the rules nothing tests.

## What is in this folder

<details class="fold">
<summary>The folders and files of <code>perturb-seq-data-format/</code></summary>

| | |
|---|---|
| `notebook.qmd`, `notebook.html` | This page and its source. `./render.sh` renders it |
| `SPEC.md` | The specification: scope, terms, and numbered statements sorted into file rules, behaviour rules and guidance |
| `RATIONALE.md` | The reasons: every choice with its alternatives and evidence, comparisons with the IGVF pipeline's format and with pertpy, planned additions, and the measurements |
| `spec/screen.json` | The machine-readable structure of a data file. The descriptions in the tree above are read from it |
| `format/` | The validator in R and in Python, with the same names, and a temporary writer |
| `example/` | Data files in the format: a high-MOI dataset, a low-MOI dataset, and a small synthetic file with every kind of column |
| `conformance/` | Data files that conform and data files that each break a rule, with what a validator must report |
| `verify/` | The verification suite |
| `scale-test/` | Recorded results of the run on 207,324 cells |

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary>How the format is defined</summary>

- **The format is `SPEC.md` and `spec/screen.json`.** The validator, `validate_screen()`, exists in R and in Python and decides whether a file conforms. There is no canonical writer.
- **A data file is read with standard libraries:** `mudata.read_h5mu` in Python, `MuData::readH5MU` in R. The format has no reader of its own.
- **Writers are custom.** Each is a wrapper around the standard writer that stays inside what both languages read correctly.

</details>
